thread.title: Turning The Quant Sails - ProShares UltraShort S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA:SDS)

author: SA Marketplace
title: Turning The Quant Sails - ProShares UltraShort S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA:SDS)
text:
2018 seems to be ending on a bad note in the markets. December is setting the wrong kind of records, and Q4 has been a bumpy one in general. This is what happens in the stock market sometimes, but it's been easy to forget over the decade-long bull market.
We're using the end of the year as a chance to lift our heads, survey the market, and see what might be coming ahead. To do so, we're inviting our Marketplace authors to do a series of roundtables. 2018 was another steady growth year for the platform, and we have a lot of great voices on the Marketplace, so we wanted to share their perspective with you.
Our Year End Marketplace Roundtable series will run through the first full market week in January. We'll feature ten different roundtable discussions, with expert panels chiming in on Tech, Energy, Dividends, Other Income strategies, Gold, Value Investing, Small-Caps, Alternative Investing Strategies, Biotech, and the Macro Outlook.
This roundtable looks at alternative investing strategies - quantitative approaches, options, and technical-driven investing. Does the renewed market volatility play into the hands of these approaches or throw a monkey wrench into the process? How much does the continued trend of passive and algo investing affect these strategies? Our panel reviews:
Rick Pendergraft , author of The Hedged Alpha Strategy Andres Cardenal, CFA , author of The Data Driven Investor ANG Traders , author of Away From The Herd Victor Dergunov , author of Albright Investment Group Yuval Taylor , author of The Stock Evaluator Stephen Castellano , author of Fundamental Momentum ChartMasterPro , author of The Options Trader Arun Chopra CMT, CFA , author of Fusion Trading Seeking Alpha: Famous last words, but it seems like 2018 marks a shift in the markets after the smooth sailing of the previous two years. What factors are most important to your investing in this climate? Rick Pendergraft: Given the shift we have seen, I think the most important thing investors can do is to stay flexible. If you are only willing to go long and if in fact we are in the beginning stages of a bear market like we saw in 2007-2009, you have to be willing to make bearish trades or move to the sidelines.
Andres Cardenal: In a market environment such as this one, capital protection should be priority number one for investors. One of the most important considerations is risk control, so you should hold an elevated cash balance in your portfolio, as well as reducing market risk by holding both long and short positions.
Victor Dergunov: It's been a phenomenal several years for stock investors, especially in the higher alpha names going into 2018. However, 2019 may be a bit different. I am looking at several factors like the Fed, global and U.S. growth, interest rates, and other factors to continuously gauge sentiment surrounding the economic atmosphere, and to assess the likely trajectory of stocks going forward.
Yuval Taylor: No matter what the investing climate may be, I always favor a low-beta strategy. When the market as a whole is going down, I expect my stock picks will go down too, but not by as much. I try to tailor my strategy to do relatively well in all markets, because I don't expect to be able to forecast market conditions.
Stephen Castellano: Relative momentum and the attractiveness of fundamentals and consensus estimate revisions will always dominate the model portfolio strategies of Fundamental Momentum. For most of 2018, simple price momentum dominated returns and fundamental-only strategies lagged, to the disappointment of many. Price momentum completely faded away by September 2018, but relative outperformance based on technical strength has increased in importance since then. In September 2018, after a few months of tinkering, I created a new model portfolio that combined technical rankings with fundamental rankings, and the resulting long/short model has significantly outperformed the fundamental-only long/short strategies since then. While I think long-only strategies will continue to underperform for at least the next few months, long/short strategies should do better, especially those that use both fundamental and technical metrics. In my opinion, this is simply because during periods of uncertainty, investors tend to sell the "show me" stocks and technically weak stocks first.
ChartMasterPro: Since I trade leveraged call and put options, adopting a disciplined stop-loss strategy will be critical to stemming any future losses. An important lesson learned the hard way (once again) over the last four weeks.
Arun Chopra: 2018 has certainly been a shift from the low volatility, trend, and momentum markets of 2017 and most of 2016. By using a multidisciplinary approach, I am relatively well prepared for these larger macro climates and regime shifts. 2018 for me was about risk management and equity market avoidance based on much of what I saw in my models in January. I've spent most of the year focusing on the dollar, relative global rates, US short-term yields, the yield curve, credit spreads, equity valuations, and especially sentiment. The dollar above say 95 represented a significant tightening, the rate of change in 2-year yields really accelerated, and the Fed's balance sheet yr over yr decline started to get close to 10%. Combined with numerous extended trends in single stocks and indexes, high valuations (especially in momentum), and excess sentiment, the risk reward went from limited to a real negative across many of the low earnings yield stocks. As we go forward, I am most concerned with where and when the Fed starts to manage and potentially pullback on this new course, how much damage has been done to date, and if we still have a broader secular bull intact. Most of my current macro work highlights intra-market relationships, commodities, currency values, and of course global monetary policy/rates. My micro work continues to focus on the 8 fusion single stock strategies, with a focus on longer-term charts, and some of the less growth and story, more balance sheet and cash flow driven fundamental factor stocks.
SA: How has the renewed market volatility this year affected your approach? Rick Pendergraft: Volatility can be beneficial when you trade options, but you have to have your timing right. I have been far more balanced between bullish and bearish trades this year than I have been in recent years.
Andres Cardenal: My approach has not changed at all, but my positioning is much more conservative and low risk because of the increase in market volatility.
Victor Dergunov: The renewed market volatility is something I had anticipated for this year. So, the theme throughout most of the year has been to rotate away from FANG, and other high multiple names, and into more defensive names and market segments. Right now, I like some select technology stocks like Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ), gold miners, some consumer staples names, Procter & Gamble ( PG ), Pfizer ( PFE ), and other defensive, stable, dividend-paying names. Additionally, I've been raising cash throughout the year, and have substantially decreased my overall equity exposure throughout the later part of 2018.
Stephen Castellano: The market volatility has not changed my approach. I just need to be more aware of intraday changes in price and volatility so I can alert subscribers when the cash allocation strategy for one particular model is triggered. Greater influence of price momentum and technical indicators forced me to take test new approaches in the middle of 2018, which helped me develop a hybrid fundamental + technical model portfolio strategy in September 2018. Interestingly, November was the first month since 2011 when moving to 100% cash for a short period of time helped returns relative to fully invested strategies.
ChartMasterPro: The bullish counter-trend trade has stopped working (buy the dip, buy support, etc.). It's more important now to identify the underlying trend of the market and trade in the direction of that trend.
Arun Chopra: The volatility really hasn't impacted my approach so much as helped validate some of the key sentiment, trend, and valuation components I focus beyond single stocks and the numbers. After such a strong and ultimately parabolic 2017, a regime switch was to be expected. This was clear in the longer-term trend data which showed some of the furthest extension from weekly levels we've seen since 2009. We also hit 60+% bulls in January, a rare reading which had only occurred post Ebola (and prior to the debt downgrade) and post QE 2 (prior to the 2015-2016 pullbacks).
You never know what the exact corrective path after a sentiment surge will be (sideways, down, etc.) and 2018 was certainly tricky, but this type of analysis suggested volatility would increase, and reward would be limited at best. Personally I was surprised it took so long (and didn't expect a new high post January), but as we know, markets work extremely hard to fool most people most of the time. To my mind, the Fed contracting the balance sheet was a game changer, especially once the amount of decline became relevant, and the post lag policy hit (generally 6-9 months). Coupled with the late cycle surge in momentum in stocks like Nvidia ( NVDA ) (16X sales at the peak) and Netflix ( NFLX ) (15X sales at the peak), I was able to short numerous trend breaks well before the larger declines. That was a big shift from 2017, and simply would not have been possible without using numerous disciplines as valuation alone, or a chart (and frankly a trend break) would not have been enough to make those trades, or see the liquidity shift.
SA: What's unique about your approach, and why is it relevant to today's market? Rick Pendergraft: This may seem like a strange answer, but I have always looked at trading and investing like being a mercenary. You have to go with the side that pays you the most money. You can't be loyal to one side or the other. If being bearish is likely to pay you more money, then you go with that side. I think too many investors fall in love with stocks and have a sense of loyalty to them. By approaching the market in such a manner, you make unemotional decisions based on what is happening, not what you want to happen.
Andres Cardenal: I use quantitative systems to protect my portfolio and reduce risk in bear markets based on factors such as trend identification and relative strength. Because of this, my portfolio has been quite protected since October, which is a massive advantage in today's market.
ANG Traders: Our working hypothesis is that the only constant in the market is the human emotion of fear - fear of losing, and fear of missing out. Fundamentals provide the "scaffolding" for the market, but fear drives the market. Fear leaves repetitive patterns in the price history of the market, which we use to determine the most probable future outcomes in the stock market. Today's market is being mispriced by irrational fear; irrational because the economy continues to expand.
Victor Dergunov: My approach is unique because I identify certain areas in the market that are likely to outperform or underperform, as well as specific stocks in those segments, and I adjust my portfolio accordingly. This has enabled my portfolio to outperform the S&P 500, and other major market averages by a substantial margin over the last year, and going back much further as well. In today's market, my approach is instrumental to beating the market because stocks are very volatile, and it is essentially a stock picker's market out there today, much more so than in prior years. Furthermore, I implement volatility and hedging strategies, including a covered call strategy on various names to substantially boost returns in the current economic environment.
Yuval Taylor: A lot of quant-based investing is founded on technical analysis or trend following; mine is based primarily on fundamentals. But at the same time, I focus on fundamental factors that other investors pay little or no attention to, and that focus gives me an edge. I'm looking for things that indicate that a company will outperform expectations, and that means looking both at factors that have historically predicted strong future performance and those that indicate misguided expectations. In today's market, we can take nothing for granted - everything we thought we knew about stock performance, from value to growth to momentum, may be, to some extent, wrong. Relying on the tried and true in an era of rapidly disseminated information may not be the best policy, for the factors that almost everyone uses will give you no edge at all. That said, you can't just forget about value, quality, or growth; in those three set of factors lie your best chances of making safe and solid investments. Instead, you have to think about them-and quantify them - in fresh and original ways.
Stephen Castellano: The model portfolio strategies I created were cutting edge for their time in the 1990s, but are now considered quaint by the PhD rocket scientists (literally speaking) dominating many quantitative investment strategies today. I suppose what is unique about the Fundamental Momentum model portfolio strategies is that despite their simplicity they continue to outperform many hedge fund long/short indices.
ChartMasterPro: In theory my trading strategy is designed to make money when markets go up and when they go down. In practice, this has not been the case over the last four weeks - market bias sneaked into my approach and skewed my trades to the long side - a painful lesson, relearned. This market bias has now been washed out of my head.
Arun Chopra: What's unique about Fusion is its multidisciplinary, incorporating macroeconomics, fundamental analysis, price action, and behavioral finance. Simply put, it's a more holistic approach to investment, portfolio management, and ultimately, risk taking. In any given year, you don't know what you are going to get, but we can bank on certain market principles from each discipline. This includes intramarket variables (such as how interest rates or currency levels impact equity), or how single stock growth and valuations drive opportunity (fundamentals), what price action across stocks, sectors and the globe suggests (technicals), and then most importantly how people behave, particularly in the context of money and markets (behavioral finance, sentiment). It's relevant because today because we are in a post GFC (global financial crisis) world, with negative rates across many countries and still low to no interest rates elsewhere. With the Fed "normalizing" both the front end and the balance sheet, many of models we have are outdated at best. To my mind this makes liquidity and market impact more important than ever. Although I am very aware of the core concepts in finance such as valuation, earnings and so forth, frankly these have to be combined with a larger "when to own" factor, particularly in the context of the cycle. This year I think has really reminded people of that.
SA: What do you enjoy about your investing strategy (beyond the returns, presumably)? Rick Pendergraft: I like the idea of being flexible with both bullish and bearish trades, short-term versus long-term trades, and stock and option trades. They don't happen all the time, but it is always fun to see a day where the market is mixed and all of your bullish positions went the right way and so did your bearish positions. If you only make bullish trades and the market drops sharply, that is frustrating.
Andres Cardenal: Investing is one of the most exciting and competitive fields in the world, and a deep passion for me. You are always analyzing the data and making decisions with important economic consequences in real time. Watching how the fundamental data, the narrative, and market prices interact over time is truly fascinating.
ANG Traders: The knowledge that fundamentals, while supporting the primary trend in the market, do not drive the market and correlate inconsistently with price movements. Fear is the driver of markets. This allows us to stay away from the herd and on the right side of the market.
Victor Dergunov: The number one thing I enjoy most about my investment strategy is being able to sleep well at night. There is nothing quite like being confident knowing that your money is working for you while you sleep and your returns are safe.
Yuval Taylor: I love investigating stock-market conundrums. Of all the things I do in my life, it's one of the most enjoyable. Back in July 2016, I made a list of questions I wanted answers to. I've reproduced them here because I've been thinking and writing about them now for close to three years, and I haven't stopped.
How much should a stock's price matter when considering an investment? Is there such a thing as a company's intrinsic value? Why isn't the market efficient? What causes the momentum effect? What is risk? Why do different measurements of growth and value produce such different results? Is there a winner for every loser? Is investing a form of gambling? What are the trade-offs in low-liquidity stock investing? Is there a logical flaw in screening stocks? What does one have to take into account when looking at a company's earnings? What is return on capital? Why is the accrual ratio important? Why is middling better than high year-to-year revenue growth? Why is a stable operating margin better than a rapidly growing one? What are the ethics of investing? Why invest in the first place? Someone once wrote that the meaning of life is puzzle-solving. That's why I love strategy development, which tries to answer these and similar questions and then puts those answers into action.
Stephen Castellano: It's tough to make buy/sell investment decisions during periods of volatility. Tracking the model portfolio updates takes out the stress of second guessing oneself because I inherently trust that each update reflects the best possible choices at that given moment.
Arun Chopra: I enjoy the overall approach because I cross over from the standard math we see in financials and finance in general, to the more social side of the market. I most enjoy behavioral finance and especially the study of psychology. Many look at charts as a sort of pseudo-science, which I get. However the combination of intra-market relationships (which is really the study of macroeconomics), trend, momentum and especially behavior, in the context of valuations and single stock business prospects is truly fascinating.
SA: What is the biggest change you've made to your investing over the past year or so? Rick Pendergraft: I can't say that my approach has changed in the past year. Because of the wild swings we have had, I have made trades on the overall market more frequently this year than in years past.
Andres Cardenal: I did not change my investing strategy or approach, but my quantitative systems are making me much more cautious since October of 2018.
Victor Dergunov: So, the biggest change has been a substantial overall reduction to equity exposure, and rotation out of the high alpha, high multiple names, and into safer, much more stable dividend paying stocks.
Yuval Taylor: I began to look at liquidity not just in terms of daily dollar volume but in terms of the bid-ask spread, and I started adjusting my position sizes accordingly, attempting to minimize my spread-related costs.
Stephen Castellano: I have always been toying with the idea of overlaying technical strategies to my fundamental strategies, but since fundamentals took a backseat to price momentum and technicals for most of 2018 I was forced out of necessity to implement a new strategy that took these into account. I will always be a fundamental analyst, but I developed a deeper appreciation for paying attention to the stock price action for it could be reflective of some underlying fundamentals that the market is discounting and which I am not yet aware of.
ChartMasterPro: At the beginning of December, I started using a customized chart of the NYSE Bullish Percentage Index (BPNYA) to identify the underlying broad market trend. This indicator worked extremely well in identifying changes in market trend since the October 1 volatility began. I will continue to use this tool going forward to determine trade bias (long or short) on individual trades based on the underlying trend identified by the BPNYA - this approach should help me stay on the right of the market.
Arun Chopra: I haven't made a real change to the approach other than continue to evolve. As with anything, more time in real world scenarios are always useful, and as with markets we know they are constantly changing. Although I knew 2018 would likely correct due to our trend extensions and sentiment in January, the path was a bit of a surprise. Although I tend to have a strong sense of what components of each discipline work well in what types of markets, I am always evaluating and adapting. This year was tough for almost everyone, trend traders, fundamental investors, even behavior was all over the map. From that standpoint I think I learned the most about my behavioral factors, and to understand that at market extremes we really need to be flexible with our rules.
SA: What are you preparing for in 2019? Any big themes to watch out for? Rick Pendergraft: I think we are probably in for more of the same in 2019. There are so many factors that are going to keep volatility levels heightened - the trade war, the Mueller investigation, the Fed's rate path, etc. One area where I will be paying particular attention is to the long-term moving averages. So many stocks, ETFs, and indices are below their 52-week moving averages and now those trendlines may act as resistance if there is a rally. That is what happened in the first part of 2008. The indices rallied up to their 52-week moving averages and then turned sharply lower from May through November.
Andres Cardenal: Definitively, it looks like 2019 could be a massively important year for the global stock markets and the economy in general. The economic deceleration in China and Europe, and its impact on the US economy will be a key factor to watch. I expect a lot of uncertainty in the credit markets, since debt levels are at record highs and liquidity is drying up. Also, I believe the so called trade war is about much more than trade, it involves important considerations in terms of world technological leadership, economic dominance, and geopolitical influence.
Victor Dergunov: I don't expect 2019 to be a blockbuster year for stocks. In fact, I expect the market to move mostly sideways to slightly lower even. There will certainly be opportunities on the long side in some individual names, but the market as a whole may have a rocky ride next year.
Stephen Castellano: Stories about high household debt levels, record stock purchases on margin, and the potential for a recession does frighten me a bit. At the same time, we are probably better prepared for a recession than we were in 2008. I think 2011 is the best analogy for 2019. I think we are going to see more volatility and market declines over the next few months, with the potential for recovery if we put the trade war, interest rate hikes, and political infighting behind us.
ChartMasterPro: Continued market volatility will be the big theme for 2019 - keeps those stops close and don't fight the trend. Trade what you see and not what you want to see.
Arun Chopra: 2019 is a big year at Fusion Point because I am planning to finally tie in my behavioral approach on a more systematic basis. Essentially all the signals and indicators I've used over a decade plus for this have been generated manually. Over 2018 I developed a more automated approach to this, due primarily to a decline in overall data costs. I will have much more on this coming up and we are already using it inside the service, but the big excitement for me is essentially scanning the market for these behavioral events vs. what I had to do in the past, which was manually locate them. Market wise as we head into 2019 much of the overbought nature I pointed to in January has been rectified; however, now we are all on the watch for stabilization of the existing secular bull versus a switch to the more secular bears we saw in say '00 and '08. I have numerous reasons to believe the jury is still out, and I find myself more recently doing the more fundamental work associated with less frothy markets.
What is one of your best ideas for 2019, and what is the story? Rick Pendergraft: Because I think most investors are still primarily long and because I am concerned about the market dropping further in 2019, I think the best idea I can give right now is to be prepared to buy an inverse ETF on the overall market. Personally I like the ProShares UltraShort S&P 500 ETF ( SDS ) because it provides leveraged inverse exposure. I wouldn't necessarily jump in right now, but I would suggest waiting for the next bounce.
Andres Cardenal: On the long side, I think Alphabet ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ) is one of the best businesses in the world. The company now has 8 different platforms with over 1 billion monthly users each and tremendous potential for growth in segments such as YouTube, Cloud, and Artificial Intelligence. Valuation is still reasonable for a company that is growing revenue at over 20% and generating an operating profit margin of more than 25%.
On the short side, the credit market could be under a lot of pain in 2019. If the economy slows down, credit spreads increase, the yield curve flattens, and credit quality deteriorates, regional banks could really suffer. I'm betting on this idea through the triple inverse leveraged regional banks ETF: Direxion Daily Regional Banks Bear 3x Shares ETF ( WDRW )
ANG Traders: Quarterhill ( QTRH ) is a holding company focused on the disciplined acquisition, management and growth of companies in dedicated technology areas. WiLAN is Quarterhill's subsidiary which manages and licenses a substantial patent portfolio. Earlier in 2018, WiLAN was award $145m by a jury in a patent suit against Apple. Even though Apple always appeals in these situations, we think there is a better than 50% chance that WiLAN's jury-win will be upheld on appeal and that Quarterhill's stock price could triple from the current price of $0.94.
Victor Dergunov: Tesla ( TSLA ), you know the story, Model 3 continuing to dominate, China factory may begin production sometime late next year, future products are in the pipeline, comparable competition still likely years away, profitability could become a constant phenomenon, etc. If there is a high-profile company capable of delivering several fold returns over the next few years (3-5), it's Tesla. Yes, I am a Tesla bull, and I stand by my story.
Yuval Taylor: In my own personal investing process, I'm slowly developing modifications to my system to take into account the fact that stocks in different sectors react differently to different factors. In some sectors, for example, R&D expenses play a major role, and in others, they don't; in some sectors, looking at the smallest companies is the best route while in others, size doesn't matter so much. I've spent years developing a very profitable one-size-fits-all approach, but I suspect it could be even more profitable if I differentiate my approach to a greater degree. As for my writing, I want to explore the different qualities and kinds of ranking systems, to work on the question of the expected returns of a strategy or stock pick, and to challenge the conventional wisdom regarding data mining. All of these will require some hard work on my part.
Stephen Castellano: My favorite idea for 2019 is Merck ( MRK ). It seems to be benefiting from strong growth of its cancer drug, Keytruda. The company is very attractive on a fundamental basis, and the stock is much more attractive on a technical basis relative to many other stocks. I think this is one of the safest and most attractive stocks you could own in 2019.
Arun Chopra: As a Fusion investor, I focus much more on fundamental factor strategies first, rather than looking at individual names to own. Looking over my 8 fundamental factors the real goal is to figure out which strategies will do well in 2019. 2017 was clearly about momentum meaning revenue growth strategies, and highly scalable business (cash kings), and strong operators (rocket stocks). Not only was monetary policy supportive, but also the trend was strong, and we saw good sentiment (as in positive, but not extreme). As we head into '19, post a momentum crash, and a renewed sense of risk, I am looking to more of the earnings driven and cash flow type strategies that characterize tougher markets. Sitting here today, it's hard to see a re-engagement of those past equity factors working without some more time to heal; however, I have no doubt the selling is impacting lesser momentum, more stable, and better valued names. I can say I am starting to see nearly 50% cash as a percentage of balance sheets on stocks, which definitely gets my attention. Ultimately these types of shifts are where I am spending most of my equity research time, while again, being very cognizant of where we are in the macro and the cycle.
